Exact recovery under a degree-restricted adversary Another interesting consequence of the above analysis is that in case we allow no corrupted vertices (i.e. M = ∅), but continue to allow an adversary to arbitrarily corrupt up to ε(deg) k edges incident to every vertex in [n], then our algorithm still achieves exact recovery and our pseudo-concentration implies that ST is always a subset of some Sℓ .14 This is interesting not only because it yields a more robust algorithm for exact recovery as described previously, but also because the used techniques might prove useful for finding algorithms in other noisy settings, including a more noisy version of RIGs where not only additional edges outside of the ground-truth cliques can form, but also some edges within the Sℓ might be missing due to noise. We leave studying this case open for future work, but believe that our techniques form a good starting point. We refer to Appendix G for more details.

Comparison to the algorithms for the FK-model Finally, we discuss how our model relates to the semi-random setting considered by Buhai et al. (2023), where algorithms robust agains a monotone adversary for the so-called Feige-Kilian model (FK-model) are introduced. Here, a clique S of size k is planted in an initially empty graph, while the edges in S × [n] \ S are present independently with probability pFK , and edges in [n] \ S × [n] \ S are entirely arbitrary. The goal is to find a list of (1 + o(1))n/k cliques that includes S. One may wonder if our model can be seen as a special case of the FK-model if the edges in [n]\S ×[n]\S are chosen appropriately and pFK is sufficiently large. While the models are certainly related, the biggest difference to our setting is that in the FK model for pFK being bounded away from 1, any clique can intersect the ground-truth S in at most O(log(n)) vertices. In RIG(n, d, p, q), 1 the typical overlap between any two Sℓ , Sℓ′ is ≈ kδ, which is of order nΩ(1) if k ⩾ n 2 +ε . To potentially be able to map between FK and RIG(n, d, p, q), we would therefore need to choose pFK quite close to one in order to achieve δk × k-sized bicliques in G[S ⊎ ([n] \ S)]. Specifically, this would require (1 − pFK )−1 ≳ δk/ log(n), as a simple calculation reveals. 1 1

statement: Here, edges within some ground truth community form with probability q ↑ while edges outside form with probability q ↓< q ↑. Can our algorithms be extended to this case? The techniques presented in Appendix F partially cover the case where up to a constant fraction of edges (that are adversarially chosen) are missing in the ground-truth Sℓ , but they do not directly extend to the twosided case. Here, a significantly larger number of missing edges has to be handled, which, however, is not adversarially chosen but random. We believe our techniques to be a good starting point for achieving recovery in RIG2 (n, d, p, q ↑, q ↓), but some further ideas will be required. Moreover, it would be interesting to see if the algorithms on RIGs with two-sided noise can still be made robust to a monotone adversary that is now not only allowed to delete edges outside of the groundtruth communities, but also to add back edges within the communities. We believe this to be the case, however it is known that the capabilities of a such adversary do shift the information-theoretic threshold for recoverability in the stochastic block model Moitra et al. (2016), so this question stil deserves a formal investigation.

Can our algorithms be extended to this case? The techniques presented in Appendix F partially cover the case where up to a constant fraction of edges (that are adversarially chosen) are missing in the ground-truth Sℓ , but they do not directly extend to the twosided case. Here, a significantly larger number of missing edges has to be handled, which, however, is not adversarially chosen but random. We believe our techniques to be a good starting point for achieving recovery in RIG2 (n, d, p, q ↑, q ↓), but some further ideas will be required. Moreover, it would be interesting to see if the algorithms on RIGs with two-sided noise can still be made robust to a monotone adversary that is now not only allowed to delete edges outside of the groundtruth communities, but also to add back edges within the communities. We believe this to be the case, however it is known that the capabilities of a such adversary do shift the information-theoretic threshold for recoverability in the stochastic block model Moitra et al. (2016), so this question stil deserves a formal investigation. Hardness of recovery in dense RIGs without noise Moreover, it would be very interesting to better understand the computational-statistical trade-offs for recovering communities in RIGs. We √ show in Appendix I that recovery is hard in the noisy model if k ≪ n like it is the case for classical planted clique. Together with the information-theoretic feasibility proved in Appendix D.1, this √ shows that there is a computational-statistical gap whenever nε ≪ k ≪ n and p, q are a sufficiently small constants. However, our reduction from planted clique in Theorem 87 crucially relies on the fact that we have independent edges outside of the communities in our model RIG(n, d, p, q). It would be very interesting to find out if this hardness carries over to the case where p is a constant and q = 0, i.e., the dense, noiseless case. We strongly believe this to be the case, however, finding evidence for a such computational statistical gap seems to be quite challenging. While there are multiple ways of giving evidence for such gaps exist (e.g. low-degree polynomials, SoS lower bounds, the overlap gap property, statistical query algorithms, reductions from other statistical problems), none of the techniques known to us seems to easily handle dense, noiseless RIGs. Finding such techniques would likely be interesting in its own right and might further shed light on other computational aspects of other average-case problems. Appendix H. Then for k ⩽ n1/2−ε the planted clique problem (Theorem 85) cannot be solved in polynomial time. Theorem 87 (Lower bound) Assume planted clique hardness Theorem 86 and let k = δn = n1/2−Ω(1) , q = Θ(1). Then there is no polynomial time algorithm that given a graph G ∼ RIG(n, d, p, q), outputs a set of d cliques that agrees with {Sℓ }ℓ∈[d] w.h.p. Proof Planting the clique. Consider a graph G′ ∼ G(n, q) and initialize K1 = ∅. Then for each vertex v ∈ V (G′ ) flip a coin such that with probability δ, v is included in K1 . Notice that by assumption E|K1 | = δn ⩽ n1/2−Ω(1) and since |K1 | is a binomial random variable it follows by a Chernoff bound that |K1 | ⩽ n1/2−Ω(1) with probability 1 − o(1). Thus, ”planting” K1 as a ′ ′ ′ K1  clique into G we obtain G1 = (V (G ), E(G ) ∪ 2 ) and thus, assuming Theorem 86, there is no polynomial time algorithm to recover K1 from G1 w.h.p. since q is non-vanishing.
